chapter_title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Building Equilateral Triangles with Compass and Ruler

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles (diagram given with one circle).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150
homework.description: Use points on two (or three) equal circles and/or their centres A, B (and C) to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.

time_bands.activity: Students attempt to place a third point by eye on a plain sheet so that all three sides of a proposed triangle look equal, then measure to check. The class discusses why guessing is unreliable, motivating a precise arc method.

Teacher models the three-step arc procedure — draw a 4 cm base, swing equal arcs from each endpoint, mark the intersection — explaining that the intersection point is equidistant from both endpoints because it lies on both arcs. Students replicate the construction for part (e) of Construct, section 7.1 p.150 ("Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.").

Students work through the remaining parts of Construct, section 7.1 p.150 ("Construct triangles with these sidelengths..."), then attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.150 ("Use points on a circle and/or its centre to form isosceles triangles..."). Pairs compare constructions and verify that sides declared equal actually measure equal.
Class-wide debrief: which parts of the construct exercise produced the neatest triangle and why? Students articulate in their own words why both AC and BC must equal the chosen arc radius.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is opening the compass to a different radius for the second arc; watch for students who reset the compass between arcs. Encourage students to measure all three sides after construction to self-check, building the habit of verification. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.150 ("Use points on two or three equal circles...") is recommended as independent follow-up for students who finish early.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

periods.activity_title: When Do Three Lengths Make a Triangle?

textbook_items_in_class.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles? Explain using the triangle inequality.

For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy 'direct length < sum of other two'? Explore. Also find which length can be identified as immediately less than the sum without calculation.

time_bands.activity: Students attempt the constructions in Math Talk, section 7.2 p.151 ("Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm...") with compass and ruler. They record what they observe when the arcs fail to meet.

Groups share their failed attempts. Teacher introduces the tent-tree-pole path metaphor: a direct path is always shorter than a detour via a third point. Students articulate this as a general statement about side lengths, working toward the triangle inequality.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.154 ("Without constructing: could you have determined that 3, 4, 8 cm and 2, 3, 6 cm cannot form triangles? Explain using the triangle inequality.") and Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.154 ("For any set of three lengths, will at least two comparisons always satisfy 'direct length < sum of other two'?"). They explore which single comparison suffices.

Students share their conjecture about the minimum number of comparisons needed. Teacher poses the question: if the longest side is less than the sum of the other two, do we need to check the other pairs? Class reasons through this together.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often believe all three triangle-inequality comparisons must be verified separately; guide them through Try This Q3 to see that only the comparison involving the longest side can fail. Watch for students who state the inequality as 'greater than' rather than 'less than'. The circle-intersection visual proof in section 7.2 — showing touching, non-intersecting, and intersecting cases — is worth referencing for students who want a more formal argument.

textbook_segments.title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given

periods.activity_title: Applying the Triangle Inequality to Construct and Classify

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine whether triangles exist for: (a) 10 km, 10 km, 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; (b) 3, 4, 6; (c) 2, 4, 8; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (f) 10, 20, 35; (g) 24, 26, 28.
For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side: (a) 1, 100; (b) 5, 5; (c) 3, 7. Describe all possible third-side values for each case.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159
homework.description: Check if a triangle exists for: (a) 1, 100, 100; (b) 3, 6, 9; (c) 1, 1, 5; (d) 5, 10, 12.

time_bands.activity: Students apply the triangle inequality to Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154 ("Determine whether triangles exist for: (a) 10 km, 10 km, 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm.") without constructing, writing a brief written justification for each decision.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.156 ("Which sets of lengths can be sidelengths of a triangle? Explain: (a) 2, 2, 5; ...") independently, then compare answers with a partner and resolve any disagreements by re-applying the inequality.

Students explore Try This Q3, section 7.2 p.159 ("For each pair of given sides, find at least 5 valid values for the third side: (a) 1, 100; (b) 5, 5; (c) 3, 7. Describe all possible third-side values..."). They write inequality expressions to describe the full range of valid third-side values.
Brief whole-class share: one student reads their inequality expression for case (c). Class confirms or corrects together.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the triangle inequality as a decision rule, students now use it fluently as a checking tool. A frequent error is describing the third side as 'any value up to the sum' without also applying the lower bound from the other pair; Try This Q3 is well-designed to surface this. Figure it Out Q1, section 7.2 p.159 is assigned for reinforcement and revisits edge cases including collinear triples.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Angle Sums, Parallel Lines, and the Angle-Sum Property

textbook_items_in_class.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the third angle (using a parallel-line argument) when two angles are: (a) 36°, 72°; (b) 150°, 15°; (c) 90°, 30°; (d) 75°, 45°.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can a triangle have all three angles equal to 70°? If two angles are 70°, what is the third? If all angles are equal, what must each be?
In triangle ABC, ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Find ∠B and ∠C.

time_bands.activity: Students carry out Math Talk, section 7.3 p.164 ("Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third...") — each student draws two different triangles, measures all three angles, and records the sums. The class pools results on the board.

Teacher presents the formal parallel-line proof: draw XY parallel to BC through A, identify the alternate angles ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C, and show that the three angles together form a straight angle at A. Students annotate their own diagrams with these labels.

Students apply the angle-sum property to Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.165 ("Find the third angle using a parallel-line argument when two angles are...") and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.165 ("Can a triangle have all three angles equal to 70°?..."), writing a one-sentence justification for each.

Students solve Try This Q3, section 7.3 p.165 ("In triangle ABC, ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Find ∠B and ∠C.") and share how they set up the equation. Class connects the angle-sum property to the existence condition explored when two base angles are supplementary.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse alternate interior angles with co-interior angles; ensure the parallel-line diagram is drawn large enough for the two pairs to be clearly distinguished. Watch for arithmetic errors when the two given angles sum close to 180°, producing a near-zero or negative third angle. Figure it Out Q2 on p.165 naturally leads students to ask about equilateral triangles, which connects to the equilateral construction from section 7.1.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Exterior Angles and Existence Conditions for Triangle Construction

textbook_items_in_class.description: Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side? Find examples where they do not.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: For each given angle (a) 30°; (b) 70°; (c) 54°; (d) 144°, find at least two angles for which a triangle is possible and two for which it is not. Find the third angle in each valid case.

Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°. Then find the exterior angle for different ∠A and ∠B values and derive the relationship between the exterior angle and the two non-adjacent interior angles.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163
homework.description: Determine which angle pairs can be two angles of a triangle: (a) 35°, 150°; (b) 70°, 30°; (c) 90°, 85°; (d) 50°, 150°.

time_bands.activity: Students investigate Math Talk, section 7.3 p.162 ("Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side?...") by constructing angle arms from base endpoints for several angle pairs. They record pairs whose arms are parallel or diverge, building a table of outcomes.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.163 ("For each given angle (a) 30°; (b) 70°; (c) 54°; (d) 144°, find at least two angles for which a triangle is possible and two for which it is not..."), using the angle-sum property established through the parallel-line proof to reason about each case.

Students compute several exterior angles in Figure it Out, section 7.3 p.166 ("Exterior angle: find ∠ACD if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°...") and record the relationship between each exterior angle and the pair of non-adjacent interior angles, expressing the pattern as a general rule.
Class articulates the exterior-angle theorem in their own words. Teacher asks: how does this relate to the angle-sum property already proven? Students connect the two results.

periods.teacher_notes: Having proved the angle-sum property via alternate angles on a parallel line, students can now derive the exterior-angle theorem as a direct corollary; prompt them to do so rather than accepting it as a new fact. A common error in Figure it Out Q1 is identifying an angle pair as valid without checking that the third angle is positive; insist on the explicit calculation. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.163 is set for homework as a straightforward application of the same reasoning.

textbook_segments.title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given

periods.activity_title: Constructing Triangles from Sides-Angle-Side and Angle-Side-Angle Data

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.
Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible? Justify from your construction observations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the four-step SAS construction: draw the base side, construct the given angle at one endpoint with a protractor, mark the second side length along the angle arm, and join the two endpoints. Students then complete Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161 ("Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.").

Students discuss Math Talk, section 7.3 p.161 ("Is there a combination of two sides and an included angle for which a triangle is not possible?...") in pairs, testing angles at or beyond 180°. They record their conclusions.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.162 ("Construct triangles given two angles and the included side: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°; (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°; (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°."), applying the ASA procedure — draw base, construct both angles from base endpoints, mark intersection C. Part (c) is examined carefully: why does the sum 120° + 30° = 150° still allow the arms to meet?
Class confirms: for ASA, the triangle fails to exist only when the two base angles sum to 180° or more. Students state this as a rule in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the angle-sum property, students can now predict existence before constructing for ASA cases — encourage this as a pre-check habit. A common error in SAS construction is measuring the included angle from the wrong arm; verify that students measure from the drawn base. For students who progress quickly, the comparison between part (c) in the SAS and ASA sets — both involving 120° — offers a productive discussion about how angle placement changes the outcome.

textbook_segments.title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles

periods.activity_title: Altitudes by Paper Folding and Set-Square Construction

textbook_items_in_class.description: Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.
Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?
Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square, for the given triangle (extended base case shown also).

time_bands.activity: Students cut out paper triangles and carry out Activity, section 7.4 p.168 ("Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base."). They compare creases with neighbours and discuss why folding a vertex onto the base produces a perpendicular crease.

Students sketch responses to Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.168 ("Visualise and draw a rough diagram: in what type of triangle is a side also an altitude?"), reasoning from the definition that an altitude is a perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side.

Teacher demonstrates the set-square-and-ruler method for Figure it Out, section 7.4 p.169 ("Construct the altitude from A to BC using ruler and set square..."), including the extended-base case where the foot of the altitude falls outside the triangle. Students practise both cases on their own triangles.
Students articulate the definition of altitude in their own words and confirm: in a right-angled triangle, the two legs are each other's altitudes.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse the altitude with the median; the paper-folding activity is effective because the crease is visibly perpendicular, making the definition concrete. Watch for students who draw the altitude only inside the triangle — the extended-base case should receive equal emphasis. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140° and construct the altitude from T") is a natural follow-on for students who finish the set-square construction quickly.

periods.activity_title: Classifying Triangles by Sides and Angles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the two classification systems — by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse) — using a simple table on the board. Students fill in the definitions in their own words and give one example of each from constructions already completed in the chapter.

Students construct the triangle and altitude for Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC."), then classify the triangle by both systems and record their classification.

Students investigate Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170 ("Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.") and record a yes/no verdict with a construction or a counter-argument for each.
Class shares verdicts for part (a) and (b): both are impossible for an equilateral triangle, since all angles must be 60°. Students state the classification constraint that rules each out.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may initially think the two classification systems are independent; Figure it Out Q4 is precisely designed to reveal the constraints between them. A common misconception is that an equilateral triangle could be right-angled — encourage students to use the angle-sum property to rule this out analytically before verifying by construction. The Try This Q3, section 7.5 p.170 on constructing a right-angled triangle from only the hypotenuse is an excellent challenge item for students who complete Q4 quickly.

periods.activity_title: Right-Angled Triangles, Hypotenuse, and the Shortest Path Puzzle

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170
textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.
Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? (Note: other measurements can take any values.)

Shortest Path in a Box: a spider at one corner of a box wants to walk (on the surfaces) to the opposite corner. Mark the shortest path on a cardboard box and compare with classmates. (Hint diagram shows unfolded surfaces.)

time_bands.activity: Students construct Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct the altitude from T to RY.") using the SAS method and then locate the altitude foot, which requires extending the base beyond the triangle.

Students tackle Try This Q3, section 7.5 p.170 ("Construct right-angled triangle ∆ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements?"). They attempt several constructions with different values for AB, and discuss whether the triangle is uniquely determined or not.

Students work on Figure it Out, section 7.5 p.172 ("Shortest Path in a Box: a spider at one corner of a box wants to walk on the surfaces to the opposite corner. Mark the shortest path on a cardboard box and compare with classmates."). They unfold a cardboard box, mark candidate paths, and compare total lengths to identify the shortest route.
Groups present their shortest-path findings. Class discusses how the triangle inequality and the idea that a straight line is the shortest path connect to the box puzzle.

periods.teacher_notes: Try This Q3 often surprises students because the hypotenuse alone does not uniquely determine a right-angled triangle — infinitely many configurations are valid. The Shortest Path puzzle connects the triangle inequality (a direct path is shorter than a detour) to a spatial problem, reinforcing the reasoning from section 7.2. Watch for students who confuse unfolding the box (producing a net) with simply measuring along the edges.

textbook_segments.title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles

periods.activity_title: Bringing It Together: Altitudes, Types, and Extended Problems

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159
textbook_items_in_class.description: Does an equilateral triangle exist with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does an equilateral triangle of any sidelength exist? Justify.

time_bands.activity: Students revisit the circle-intersection framework from section 7.2 via Figure it Out, section 7.2 p.158 ("Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle."). They articulate the full procedure — longest-side check, then arc construction — as a numbered algorithm.

Students answer Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159 ("Does an equilateral triangle exist with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does an equilateral triangle of any sidelength exist? Justify."), connecting the triangle inequality proof to the equilateral case — showing that for equal sides, each side equals the sum of the other two minus one side, so the inequality is always strictly satisfied.

Students choose one triangle from section 7.5 that they have not yet constructed with an altitude — a scalene obtuse triangle — and produce both the triangle (using ASA or SAS) and the altitude from the vertex opposite the longest side, extending the base as necessary. They classify the result by both systems.

Students write a brief statement: given only two angles and a side, what conditions on the angles ensure a triangle can be constructed? They connect this to the angle-sum property proven via the parallel-line argument in section 7.3.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the arc-intersection reasoning from section 7.2, the angle-sum property from section 7.3, and the altitude construction from section 7.4 — naming these by their content rather than their position helps students see the chapter as a coherent set of tools rather than separate topics. Watch for students who assume an obtuse triangle's altitude always lands inside the triangle; the extended-base construction is the key correction. Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.159 is a strong closing exercise because it requires students to reason generally rather than numerically.

items.prompt: A triangle has sides of lengths 5 cm, 5 cm, and 7 cm. Which of the following correctly classifies this triangle by both its sides and its angles?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The triangle is isosceles (two sides equal: 5 cm, 5 cm) and acute-angled (all three angles are less than 90°, since the longest side squared is 49, which is less than 25 + 25 = 50).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the side-classification definition (two equal sides → isosceles) and verify the angle classification using the angle-sum property and the relative sizes of sides.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student knows the triangle is not scalene but confuses equilateral (all three sides equal) with isosceles (exactly two sides equal).
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly identifies both the side and angle classification.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly identifies the side type but incorrectly judges the triangle as obtuse, possibly by assuming the unequal side is opposite the largest angle and overestimating that angle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses isosceles with scalene, failing to notice that two sides are equal.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to measure and list the three sides, then look back at the definitions of equilateral, isosceles, and scalene to decide which fits.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the definitions of all six triangle types and provide one example of each that they construct themselves.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.170
exercise.description: Construct triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct the altitude from A to BC.

items.prompt: Which of the following combinations of triangle type is impossible?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A right-angled equilateral triangle is impossible. In an equilateral triangle all three angles must be equal and sum to 180°, so each angle is 60°; none can be 90°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-sum property: if a triangle is equilateral all angles are 60°, so no angle can be 90° or greater.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student knows right-angled isosceles triangles exist (two 45° angles and one 90°) and correctly does not choose this.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student knows obtuse isosceles triangles exist (e.g., two base angles of 30° and apex 120°) and correctly does not choose this.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student knows equilateral triangles have three 60° angles and are therefore always acute, correctly rejecting this as impossible.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly identifies that an equilateral triangle cannot have a right angle, since all its angles are 60°.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the definition of equilateral and the angle-sum property and write out the angles of an equilateral triangle before deciding.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to name one more impossible combination (e.g., obtuse-angled equilateral) and explain why using the angle-sum property.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.5 p.170
exercise.description: Through construction, explore whether it is possible to construct: (a) a right-angled equilateral triangle; (b) an obtuse-angled equilateral triangle; (c) a right-angled isosceles triangle; (d) an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: A student claims: 'If the sum of the two shorter sides of three given lengths equals the longest side, a triangle can still be formed.' Is the student correct? Justify your answer using the triangle inequality.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student is incorrect. The triangle inequality requires each side to be strictly less than the sum of the other two. If the longest side equals the sum of the other two, the two arcs will just touch at one point and no triangle is formed — the three lengths are collinear.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the triangle inequality: the longest side must be strictly less than the sum of the other two; equality gives collinear points, not a triangle.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to try constructing arcs for lengths 3, 4, 7 and observe what happens — the two circles touch rather than intersect.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what if the longest side is greater than the sum of the other two — where do the arcs end up, and what does that tell you?

exercise.description: Attempt to construct triangles with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, 8 cm and 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm. Find more sets of lengths for which a triangle is impossible, and identify a pattern.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: In triangle PQR, ∠P = 65° and ∠Q = 75°. Using the angle-sum property, find ∠R. Then explain, using the parallel-line argument, why the three angles of any triangle must sum to 180°.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ∠R = 180° − 65° − 75° = 40°. The parallel-line argument: draw a line XY through vertex A parallel to BC. The alternate interior angles give ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C. At A, ∠XAB + ∠BAC + ∠YAC = 180° (angles on a straight line), so ∠B + ∠A + ∠C = 180°, i.e., the three angles of any triangle sum to 180°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the angle-sum property (∠P + ∠Q + ∠R = 180°) and justify it via the parallel-line construction identifying alternate angles.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to draw a triangle, draw a line parallel to the base through the top vertex, and label the alternate angles before attempting the written explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if one angle of a triangle is altered by 10°, exactly how does the sum of the other two change, and what does this tell you about the angle-sum property?

exercise.description: Experiment with different triangles to find a relation between any two angles and the third. What data will you track and how will you organise it?

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: Two angles of a triangle are given as 95° and 90°. Explain, using the angle-sum property, why no triangle can be formed with these two angles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two given angles sum to 95° + 90° = 185°, which already exceeds 180°. Since the three angles of any triangle must sum to exactly 180°, there is no positive value left for the third angle, so no triangle can exist.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-sum property: if two angles already exceed 180° together, the third angle would have to be negative, which is impossible.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first add the two given angles and compare the result with 180° before drawing any conclusion.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: change one of the two angles so that a triangle becomes just barely possible — what is the boundary condition, and what kind of triangle would result?

exercise.description: Do triangles always exist for every combination of two angles and the included side? Find examples where they do not.

items.prompt: Using only a compass and ruler, describe the steps to construct a triangle with all three sides equal to 6 cm. Then verify, using the arc-radius argument, that both non-base sides are indeed 6 cm.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Steps: (1) Draw base AB = 6 cm. (2) Open compass to 6 cm and draw an arc centred at A. (3) Without changing the compass, draw an arc centred at B. (4) Mark point C at the intersection of the two arcs. (5) Draw AC and BC. Verification: C lies on the arc of radius 6 cm centred at A, so AC = 6 cm. C also lies on the arc of radius 6 cm centred at B, so BC = 6 cm. Both non-base sides equal the base, confirming the triangle is equilateral.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the equal-arc construction: each arc has radius equal to the base, so both non-base sides inherit that radius by the definition of a circle.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to draw the construction first and then measure AC and BC with a ruler before writing the arc-radius argument.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if you constructed the same arc procedure using a radius different from the base length — say the base is 6 cm but the arcs have radius 4 cm — what triangle would result, and how would you classify it?

exercise.description: Construct triangles with these sidelengths (all in cm) using compass and ruler: (a) 4, 4, 6; (b) 3, 4, 5; (c) 1, 5, 5; (d) 4, 6, 8; (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5.

items.section_title: Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
items.prompt: Three lengths are given: 8 cm, 5 cm, and 14 cm. Without constructing, determine whether a triangle is possible. Show your working using the triangle inequality. If a triangle is possible, state which arc-intersection case (intersecting, touching, or non-intersecting) would appear.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Check the critical comparison: the longest side is 14 cm. Sum of the other two: 8 + 5 = 13 cm. Since 14 > 13, the longest side exceeds the sum of the other two. The triangle inequality is violated. No triangle is possible. If constructed, the arcs centred at the two base endpoints would not intersect — the circles would be non-intersecting (the longer arc falls short of reaching the shorter one).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the longest side with the sum of the other two; since 14 > 8 + 5, the inequality fails and no triangle exists.

inclusivity.support: Draw an empty number line and mark 13 and 14 on it to make the comparison between the sum and the longest side visually clear.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the complete range of valid third-side values if the two given sides are 5 cm and 8 cm, and state the answer as an inequality.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.2 p.154
exercise.description: Determine whether triangles exist for: (a) 10 km, 10 km, 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm, 40 cm.

items.section_title: Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
items.prompt: Describe the steps to construct a triangle with two sides of 5 cm and 8 cm and an included angle of 50°. Then find the third angle if the other two angles of the triangle are 50° and 80°.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Construction steps (SAS): (1) Draw base AB = 8 cm. (2) At A, use a protractor to mark an angle of 50°. (3) Along the angle arm from A, mark point C at 5 cm. (4) Draw BC to complete the triangle. Third angle: ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°; if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 80°, then ∠C = 180° − 50° − 80° = 50°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the four-step SAS construction procedure, then use the angle-sum property to find the third angle.

inclusivity.support: Provide the student with a partially drawn base and ask them to complete only the angle and arc steps before computing the third angle.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the included angle to 130° and ask the student to predict, before constructing, how the shape and size of the triangle change compared to the 50° version.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.161
exercise.description: Construct triangles given two sides and the included angle: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm; (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm; (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm.

items.section_title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles
items.prompt: A triangle has a base along a horizontal line and the opposite vertex above the base. Describe how you would use a set square and ruler to construct the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Then explain why the paper-folding method also produces a perpendicular to the base.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Set-square method: align the ruler along the base; place the set square with one of its right-angle edges against the ruler; slide the set square along the ruler until its vertical edge passes through the top vertex; draw the segment from the vertex down to the base along the vertical edge — this is the altitude. Paper-folding: when the top vertex is folded onto the base, the crease lies equidistant from every pair of corresponding points on the two layers; this equal-distance property means the crease is perpendicular to the base at the foot.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the set-square right angle to guarantee perpendicularity; explain the fold crease as the locus of points equidistant from the vertex and its reflection.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to carry out the paper-folding activity first and then describe in their own words what the crease represents before writing the explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: for an obtuse triangle, the foot of the altitude falls outside the triangle — describe how you would extend the base and adjust the set-square procedure to handle this case.

exercise.description: Altitudes Using Paper Folding: cut out a paper triangle, fix one side as the base, and fold so the crease is the altitude from the top vertex to the base. Justify why the crease is perpendicular to the base.

items.section_title: Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles
items.prompt:
Three side-length sets are listed below. For each, state without constructing whether a triangle exists, and justify your answer. Then, for the one set that does form a triangle, state what type it is by sides.

| Set | Side lengths |
|-----|--------------|
| (a) | 6, 6, 11     |
| (b) | 4, 7, 12     |
| (c) | 9, 9, 9      |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 6 + 6 = 12 > 11: triangle exists. Type: isosceles. (b) 4 + 7 = 11 < 12: longest side 12 exceeds sum of other two; no triangle. (c) 9 + 9 = 18 > 9: triangle exists. Type: equilateral. So sets (a) and (c) form triangles; set (b) does not.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For each set, compare the longest side with the sum of the other two using the triangle inequality, then classify the valid triangles by the side-equality definition.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to identify the longest side in each set first and write it down, then compute the sum of the remaining two before comparing.
inclusivity.challenge: For set (a), ask the student to find the range of all valid third-side values when the two given sides are both 6 cm, expressing the answer as a compound inequality.

exercise.description: Find 3 examples each of sidelength sets where the two circles: (a) touch each other at a point; (b) do not intersect. Frame a complete procedure to check the existence of a triangle.
